clue.text: Dating advert redrafted for father of

indicators.note: a draft rewritten has its contents put into a new order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A lonely-hearts notice is rewritten on behalf of somebody's father.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue as held ends 'father of', with the cross-reference evidently lost in print: the novelist wrote A Man in the Zoo (1924), the answer at 26 across.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bloomsbury novelist was the author, figuratively the parent, of the 1924 novel at 26 across.

clue.text: Unexpectedly raid little review for drawing

indicators.note: something done unexpectedly takes an unforeseen turn, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: a mag is a short form of magazine, a review in miniature

explanation.surface: A surprise police raid turns up a small magazine with a sketch in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unexpectedly' rearranges RAID together with MAG, the clipped word for a magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: A diagram is a plan or sketch, a kind of drawing.

clue.text: A Madelaine with a past, predating proust

definitions.text: A Madelaine with a past, predating proust

parts.words: A Madelaine with a past, predating proust
parts.note: Hugo's escaped convict lived under the alias Monsieur Madeleine, a respectable mayor hiding a criminal past, decades before Proust made the madeleine cake famous

explanation.surface: A little cake with a history, older than the famous one dipped in tea.
explanation.walkthrough: The spelling and Proust point to the cake; the man is the hero of Les Misérables (1862), who took the name Madeleine.
explanation.definitionFit: Hugo's hero calls himself Monsieur Madeleine while concealing his years in the galleys.

clue.text: A bit of a comedown for a man of letters

definitions.text: A bit of a comedown for a man of letters

parts.words: A bit of a comedown for a man of letters
parts.note: in typography, the stroke of a printed letter such as p or g that drops below the line is a part that comes down

explanation.surface: A writer suffers a minor humiliation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'man of letters' suggests a writer, but the letters are printed characters and the comedown is the tail falling below the baseline.
explanation.definitionFit: In printing, the downward tail of a letter below the line is so named because it goes down.

clue.text: A pound worker for playwright

parts.note: L stands for the pound sterling, from Latin libra
a worker is a bee in the hive

explanation.surface: A pound paid to a labourer on behalf of a dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worker' is the crossword's usual worker bee.
explanation.definitionFit: Edward Albee was the American dramatist of Who's Afraid of Virginia Woolf?

clue.text: Carer on railway, describing Elgar piece

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece placed on another sits above it, so the carer comes first

parts.note: a nurse is someone who cares for the sick

explanation.surface: A nurse travelling by train describes a piece of Elgar's music.
explanation.walkthrough: The word describes the piece rather than naming all of it: Elgar's Nursery Suite (1931).
explanation.definitionFit: Elgar's late orchestral work for the royal princesses is the Nursery Suite, so the word stands for that composition.

clue.text: There have been those under the moon who were more welcome

definitions.text: There have been those under the moon who were more welcome

parts.words: There have been those under the moon who were more welcome
parts.note: Oberon greets his fairy queen with 'Ill met by moonlight', so others met under the moon have been better met

explanation.surface: Some people, met by moonlight, were greeted more warmly.
explanation.walkthrough: The line is from A Midsummer Night's Dream: 'Ill met by moonlight, proud' queen of the fairies.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's fairy queen is the one Oberon calls 'ill met by moonlight', a less welcome meeting than others.

clue.text: Anti-novelist who exhibited jealousy in 1957

parts.note: the leading French nouveau roman writer published La Jalousie in 1957

explanation.surface: A writer opposed to novels showed envy in the late fifties.
explanation.walkthrough: Jealousy here is a book title, La Jalousie, not an emotion shown by the writer.
explanation.definitionFit: The French nouveau roman pioneer wrote La Jalousie (1957) and was called an anti-novelist.

clue.text: They looked to the future in Kennedy's work

definitions.text: They looked to the future in Kennedy's work

parts.words: They looked to the future in Kennedy's work
parts.note: Margaret Kennedy's 1955 novel takes its title from prophets who foretell what is to come

explanation.surface: People in a Kennedy administration who planned ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: Kennedy suggests the American president; it is the novelist Margaret Kennedy, whose novel The Oracles appeared in 1955.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient prophets and shrines that foretold events were the subject of Margaret Kennedy's novel title.

clue.text: All-found accommodation for young Irish writer

definitions.text: All-found accommodation for young Irish writer

parts.words: All-found accommodation for young Irish writer
parts.note: Brendan Behan was sent as a teenager to a British young offenders' institution, recounted in ... Boy, with board and lodging provided

explanation.surface: Free board and lodging offered to a budding Irish author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'All-found' means bed and board supplied; Behan's lodging was a British young offenders' institution, as told in Borstal Boy (1958).
explanation.definitionFit: A British reform institution for young offenders housed the teenage Behan, as his memoir title records.

clue.text: 7's homage to amaze, say

parts.note: the French novelist at 7 down wrote Dans ..., a book whose very title means 'in the maze'

explanation.surface: A tribute from the writer at 7 meant to astonish readers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'amaze' splits as 'a maze': the novel at 7 down is Dans le labyrinthe (1959), French for 'in the labyrinth'.
explanation.definitionFit: The French word for a maze, with its article, forms part of the title of the 1959 novel.

clue.text: Orwell's days

parts.note: Orwell's first novel, set in colonial Burma, is titled after days spent there

explanation.surface: The time George Orwell lived through.
explanation.walkthrough: Orwell's first novel is Burmese Days (1934), drawn from his police service in Burma.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective for things from Burma, now Myanmar, is the first word of Orwell's novel title.

clue.text: Lasting orders of Manning

definitions.meaning: Cardinal Manning's book on the priesthood, holy orders

explanation.surface: A permanent set of instructions from Manning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'orders' means holy orders, the priesthood; Cardinal Manning wrote The Eternal Priesthood (1883).
explanation.definitionFit: Something everlasting is without end; Manning's treatise on holy orders bears that adjective in its title.

clue.text: "There are little —s mocking them" (Thackeray, Paris Sketch Book)

definitions.text: "There are little —s mocking them" (Thackeray, Paris Sketch Book)

parts.words: "There are little —s mocking them" (Thackeray, Paris Sketch Book)
parts.note: the gap in Thackeray's sentence takes the French word for a street urchin of Paris

explanation.surface: A quotation from Thackeray's account of Paris with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in clue: the missing word, used in English since the 1830s, is the Parisian street boy.
explanation.definitionFit: A street urchin, a ragged boy of the Paris streets, fits the mockers in Thackeray's sketch.

clue.text: Your old place in terrible dim bar suggests hymn to Bacchus

indicators.note: to place one thing in another is to set it inside, so the old word goes within the jumbled letters
something terrible is in a bad state, so these letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: thy is the old form of your

explanation.surface: A dreadful dingy bar is where you once drank, and it calls for a song to the wine god.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terrible' rearranges DIM BAR into DIRAMB, and 'place in' puts THY (archaic 'your') inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A dithyramb was a wild choral song in honour of Dionysus, the Bacchus of the Romans.

clue.text: Bush follower ready to communicate

definitions.meaning: the word follows bush in the phrase for rumour spreading by word of mouth
the device or verb for sending messages over a distance, or signalling in advance

explanation.surface: A supporter of President Bush is keen to talk.
explanation.walkthrough: Bush looks like the US president; it is the bush of the 'bush telegraph', informal word-of-mouth news.
explanation.definitionFit: The bush telegraph is the grapevine, and the instrument sends messages by wire, a means of communication.

clue.text: Original deployment of characters making Gaul a ruin

indicators.note: the letters are deployed afresh, set out in new positions like troops, so the phrase is rearranged

explanation.surface: Caesar's first campaign through Gaul leaves the province ruined.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deployment of characters' rearranges GAUL A RUIN; 'making' is the link to the definition, which comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: An inaugural event is the first of its kind, the one that originates a series.

clue.text: Opposite a Roman commander over a thousand…

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece over another is written above it, so the general comes first

parts.note: Mark Antony was the Roman general
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand

explanation.surface: Facing a Roman general who commands more than a thousand men.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue runs on into 18 down: the next clue continues its sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A word's antonym is the word of contrary meaning, its opposite.

clue.text: … not cut by Greek one we're told!

definitions.text: … not cut by Greek one we're told!

parts.words: … not cut by Greek one we're told!
parts.note: 'not' sounds like knot, and the Greek one is Alexander, who cut through the famous Phrygian knot

explanation.surface: Continuing 17: a Roman commander not wounded by a Greek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we're told' turns 'not' into 'knot': Alexander the Great sliced the knot tied by King Gordius.
explanation.definitionFit: The knot of Gordius, cut by Alexander, is the adjective's famous partner.

clue.text: More depressed, perhaps, than Mrs Molesworth's baby

definitions.text: More depressed, perhaps, than Mrs Molesworth's baby

parts.words: More depressed, perhaps, than Mrs Molesworth's baby
parts.note: Mrs Molesworth wrote The Blue Baby, so something more of that colour, or sadder, outdoes her baby

explanation.surface: Someone in lower spirits than an infant in a Victorian children's book.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Molesworth, a Victorian children's author, wrote The Blue Baby; blue also means sad.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling blue means feeling low, so the comparative means sadder, and also more blue in colour than the baby.

clue.text: Composer suggests rail disaster in Dickens

indicators.note: one piece goes in the other, set within the pen name

parts.note: Boz was the pen name of Charles Dickens

indicators.note: a disaster wrecks things, so the letters of the word are scrambled

parts.note: the printed fodder, whose letters should be R, I, L and E for the parse to work

explanation.surface: A composer hints at a train crash in a Dickens novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Setter's slip: 'disaster' should rearrange the fodder into ERLI to go 'in' BOZ, Dickens's pen name, but RAIL has an A where an E is needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Hector Berlioz was the French Romantic composer of the Symphonie fantastique.

clue.text: Philosopher seems masculine among some Spanish ones

indicators.note: one letter placed among others goes between them

parts.note: una is the feminine Spanish word for one
uno is the masculine Spanish word for one

explanation.surface: A thinker seems manly among a few Spaniards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some Spanish ones' gives two forms of 'one', UNA and UNO, and M goes 'among' them.
explanation.definitionFit: Miguel de Unamuno was the Spanish philosopher of The Tragic Sense of Life.

clue.text: How dead conducted Roman church

parts.note: the late means the dead, as in 'the late king'
to run a business is to conduct it

explanation.surface: How a dead man led a service in a Roman church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'late' is the usual crossword word for dead; St John Lateran is the cathedral of Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: St John Lateran is the cathedral church of the bishop of Rome.

clue.text: Some very thin stuff from subject of Parker verse

definitions.meaning: a sheer lightweight silk or nylon fabric
Dorothy Parker wrote a poem on the French courtesan ... de l'Enclos

explanation.surface: Flimsy material from the topic of a Dorothy Parker poem.
explanation.walkthrough: Parker is Dorothy Parker, whose 'Ninon de l'Enclos, on her last birthday' addresses the 17th-century courtesan.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheer dress fabric shares its name with the French courtesan of Parker's poem.

clue.text: 'Edie… did not venture to repeat a query which was so little —— to the matter' (Scott, The Antiquary)

definitions.text: 'Edie… did not venture to repeat a query which was so little —— to the matter' (Scott, The Antiquary)

parts.words: 'Edie… did not venture to repeat a query which was so little —— to the matter' (Scott, The Antiquary)
parts.note: Scott's gap takes an old spelling of the word for relevant or pertinent

explanation.surface: A line from Scott's novel with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in clue: Scott uses the older spelling with -ain of the word now spelt -ane.
explanation.definitionFit: The older form of a word meaning relevant or pertinent fits Edie's query that had no bearing on the matter.

clue.text: Sonnet I rewrote to provide some suspense

indicators.note: a poem rewritten has its words rearranged, so these letters are set out anew

explanation.surface: A poet redrafts a sonnet to build up suspense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rewrote' rearranges SONNET I; 'to provide' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tension is the strain of uncertainty, the feeling suspense creates.

clue.text: A measure of Two on a Tower?

definitions.text: A measure of Two on a Tower?

parts.words: A measure of Two on a Tower?
parts.note: Hardy's novel follows an amateur astronomer on a tower, and astronomers measure the angle of a star around the horizon

explanation.surface: How tall is a couple standing on a tower?
explanation.walkthrough: Two on a Tower (1882) is Hardy's novel of an astronomer; the measure is the angular bearing used to locate a star.
explanation.definitionFit: An astronomer's angle round the horizon from north locates a star, a measurement suited to Hardy's stargazers.

clue.text: One of Angus Wilson's senior citizens born in 1924?

definitions.text: One of Angus Wilson's senior citizens born in 1924?

parts.words: One of Angus Wilson's senior citizens born in 1924?
parts.note: Wilson wrote The Old Men at the Zoo (1961), and David Garnett's novel of a man caged as an exhibit appeared in 1924

explanation.surface: An elderly character from an Angus Wilson novel whose birth year was 1924.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilson's novel is The Old Men at the Zoo (1961); the singular figure was 'born' in 1924 as David Garnett's novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Garnett's 1924 novel title describes a single man on display, one of the old men in Wilson's zoo.
